text: Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016). Industrial and commercial establishments in Sindh employing 10 or more workers (now, or on any day in the previous 12 months), plus classes notified by Government. Not applicable where government statutory service rules apply. Some Standing Orders (e.g. SO 13 bonus, SO 15 closure) do not initially apply to industrial establishments with 20 or fewer persons. Official text: https://lhr.sindh.gov.pk/storage/rulesRegulations/6jLG9Ha7bNMwJgKNpGyxfmIVa4YzXmeLAvV60TXW.pdf Caveats: Applies only where 10 or more workers are employed - confirm the size of the establishment first. If the employer operates in more than one province (trans-provincial), federal law and the NIRC may apply instead of Sindh forums - see federal-industrial-relations-2012.
Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), s.1(4): Applies to industrial and commercial establishments with 10 or more workers.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), s.2(1)(n): 'Worker' includes permanent, probationer, badli, temporary, apprentice and contract workers, but not an occupier or manager who has hiring and firing authority.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), s.5: The employer must display the Act in English, Urdu and Sindhi (and in the language of the majority of workers) near the entrance and in all departments.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), s.7: Contravening the Standing Orders is punishable with fines; prosecutions are brought by the Inspector and tried by the Labour Court.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), s.11: No discrimination on the basis of gender, religion, political affiliation, sect, colour, caste, creed or ethnic background in enforcing the Act.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 1: Classes of worker: permanent, probationer, badli, temporary, apprentice, contract worker (seasonal worker added in 2021). Probation is 3 months; a worker engaged on work likely to last more than 9 months becomes permanent after satisfactorily completing 3 months' probation. Temporary work is work likely to finish within 9 months.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 3: Every worker must be given an appointment letter at the time of appointment stating the terms and conditions of employment, including wages. Transfers and promotions must also be given in writing.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 9: Paid holidays and leave apply as provided by law; all festival holidays declared by Government are paid. A leave application must be decided within a week, and a refusal must be recorded in writing with reasons.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 10(2): Wages must be paid before the 7th day after the wage period ends (establishments with up to 1,000 workers) or before the 10th day (more than 1,000 workers).

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 10(3): In commercial establishments, work beyond 9 hours a day or 48 hours a week must be paid at twice the normal wage rate.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 12: Establishments with 20 or more workers must insure all permanent workers (group insurance) against natural death, disability, and death or injury not covered by workmen's compensation or social security law; if the employer fails, the employer pays the equivalent amount.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 14(3): Workers laid off because of plant failure, curtailment of production or similar causes get half their daily wages as compensation for the first 14 days of lay-off.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 15: An employer may not terminate more than 50% of the workers or close the whole establishment without prior Government permission (except for fire, catastrophe, power stoppage, epidemic or civil commotion).

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 16(1): Terminating a permanent worker for any reason other than misconduct requires one month's notice, or one month's wages (average of the last 3 months) in lieu. The same one-month notice applies when a permanent worker leaves.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 16(2): Temporary workers, probationers, badlis and contract workers are not entitled to notice of termination (and need not give notice when leaving).

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 16(3): No worker may be terminated, removed, retrenched, discharged or dismissed except by a written order that explicitly states the reason. An aggrieved worker can use the individual grievance procedure of the Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013. Note: The Standing Order cross-refers to 'section 37' of the Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013; the grievance section of that Act is s.34, and High Court of Sindh judgments apply s.34 together with SO 16(3).

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 16(4): On termination, earned wages and other dues (including payment for unavailed leave) must be paid before the end of the second working day.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 16(6): On resignation, or on termination for any reason other than misconduct, the worker gets gratuity of one month's wages for every completed year of service (or part of a year above 6 months) - unless, for that period, the employer ran a provident fund with an employer contribution at least equal to the worker's (and the provident fund amount is not less than the gratuity). Note: Wording as amended by Sindh Act No. XXVIII of 2021 (seasonal-worker proviso removed).

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 16(7): A worker is entitled to the full provident fund balance, including the employer's contributions, even after resigning or being dismissed.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 16(10): If a worker is not allowed to work or to mark attendance, the worker may report this in writing to the area Inspector within 10 days; the employer is then barred from initiating action against the worker.
Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 17: A permanent worker is entitled to a service certificate when the employment ends for any reason.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 18-19: Retrenchment within a category is last-come, first-go; retrenched workers get preference if the employer hires again within one year.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 20-A: A seasonal worker who worked throughout the season (at least 75% of its days) gets one extra month's wages at the end of the season.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 21(3): Misconduct includes wilful insubordination, theft, fraud or dishonesty, wilful damage, bribery, habitual absence or absence without leave for more than 10 days, habitual late attendance, riotous behaviour, habitual negligence, illegal strike and go-slow.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 21(4): No dismissal for misconduct unless the worker is informed in writing of the alleged misconduct within one month and given a chance to explain; an independent inquiry is required and the worker may nominate a co-worker to assist.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 21(5): Suspension pending inquiry may not exceed one week at a time or four weeks in total (with limited exceptions), and full wages are payable during suspension.

Sindh Terms of Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XI of 2016), SO 22: A worker occupying employer-provided housing must vacate it within 2 months after the employment ends; after that the employer may seek summary eviction from a First Class Magistrate.

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017). Persons employed in factories, industrial and commercial establishments, mines and railways in Sindh. Official text: https://lhr.sindh.gov.pk/storage/rulesRegulations/nCSYViYCle1TPJp9l2vjT8bUbh5aEXngBNAtxvN2.pdf Caveats: The Authority for each area is notified by Government; the Sindh Labour Department can say which office handles a given district. A separate 6-month claim route exists for minimum-wage shortfalls (see sindh-minimum-wages-2015, s.10).

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.2(1)(b): Covers commercial establishments including banks, insurance companies, clubs, hotels, restaurants, departmental stores, cinemas, schools, colleges and private educational institutions, hospitals, private health centres and clinical laboratories, and private security agencies run on a commercial basis.

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.2(1)(d): 'Employed person' includes permanent, probationer, badli, temporary, apprentice and contract workers, but not an occupier or manager with hiring and firing authority.
Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.3: Every employer, including a contractor, is responsible for paying the wages of persons employed by them.
Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.4: The employer fixes wage periods; no wage period may exceed one month.

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.5(1): Wages must be paid before the 7th day after the wage period (where fewer than 1,000 persons are employed) or before the 10th day (others), on a working day.
Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.5(2): When the employer terminates employment, earned wages must be paid before the end of the second working day.
Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.6: Wages must be paid through a crossed cheque or bank transfer, together with a pay slip showing the details.

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.7: Only listed deductions are allowed: fines, absence, damage or loss caused by the worker's neglect, approved amenities or services, recovery of advances or overpayments, income tax, court orders, provident fund, and approved co-operative or insurance payments.

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.8: Fines only for acts or omissions approved and displayed in a notice, and only after a chance to show cause; total fines in one wage period cannot exceed 3% of wages, and cannot be recovered in instalments or after 60 days.

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.15(1): Claims about illegal deductions, delayed wages, or unpaid provident fund or gratuity dues are decided by an Authority notified for the area (a Commissioner for Workmen's Compensation or a Directorate of Labour officer of at least grade 18).

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.15(2): The worker, a lawyer, an authorised trade union official, a Labour Inspector or the worker's heirs may apply, within 3 years of the deduction or of the date the wages were due (later only if sufficient cause is shown).

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.15(3): The Authority can order refund or payment plus compensation of up to 10 times the amount deducted (no compensation for delay caused by a bona fide error or dispute, an emergency, or the worker's failure to collect).
Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.15(4): A malicious or vexatious applicant can be ordered to pay the employer a penalty of up to Rs 5,000.

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.16: One application can cover a group of workers of the same establishment whose wages for the same period are unpaid; in a group application compensation is capped at Rs 10 per worker.

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.17: Appeal against the Authority's direction lies to the Labour Court within 30 days (an employer must first deposit the amount ordered).

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.20(3): Discrimination in wages between men and women is punishable with a fine of Rs 20,000 to 50,000 (Rs 50,000 to 75,000 for a repeat offence).
Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.23: Any contract or agreement by which a worker gives up rights under this Act is void to that extent.
Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.24: On closure, insolvency, winding up or liquidation, workers' dues (wages, gratuity, provident fund) are recovered from the proceeds.

Sindh Payment of Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VI of 2017), s.25: No discrimination on grounds of sex, religion, descent, tribe, political affiliation, sect, colour, caste, creed or ethnic background in enforcing the Act.

Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016). All industrial and commercial establishments in Sindh. Official text: https://humanrights.sindh.gov.pk/storage/rulesRegulations/fqVb7dOULaCVv7WKLUJibqYWQVV0IKcgQ18EWhLc.pdf Caveats: Never hardcode the rate - read the current figure from current_rates.json. The 2018 amendment has not been reviewed yet.
Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.1(3): Applies to all industrial establishments and commercial establishments in Sindh.
Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.2(ii)-(iii): An adolescent is a person aged 14 to under 18; an adult is 18 or older.

Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.2(vi): 'Commercial establishment' includes banks, insurance companies, clubs, hotels, restaurants, cinemas, schools, colleges, private educational institutions, hospitals, private health centres, laboratories and private security agencies run on a commercial basis; the Act also applies to employees of registered societies and voluntary social welfare organisations.
Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.2(xv): Minimum wages include basic pay plus statutory allowances (cost of living allowance, dearness allowance and ad hoc relief).

Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.2(xx): 'Worker' excludes Federal and Provincial Government employees and persons employed in an employer capacity or notified as occupier/manager.

Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.6: Minimum rates are recommended by the Minimum Wages Board and declared by Government notification in the official Gazette; they take effect on publication unless another date is given.
Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.9(1): No employer may pay a worker less than the declared minimum rate (subject only to authorised deductions).
Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.9(2): Workers already entitled to higher wages under an agreement, contract, award or custom keep the higher wages.

Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.9(3): Paying below the minimum rate is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine of Rs 20,000 to 50,000, or both - plus paying the worker the shortfall.

Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.10: An Authority notified for the area hears claims for non-payment or delayed payment of minimum wages; the worker (or someone authorised) applies within 6 months of the due date (up to 1 year with sufficient cause); the Authority can order payment plus a penalty of up to 10 times the wages withheld.
Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.11: Appeal against the Authority's order lies to the Labour Court within 30 days.

Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.14: Factory and shop inspectors are also inspectors under this Act (shop inspectors for shops and establishments with 9 or fewer workers).

Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.15(4): Discriminating between men and women in paying minimum wages is punishable with a fine of Rs 20,000 to 50,000 (Rs 50,000 to 75,000 for a repeat offence).

Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. VIII of 2016), s.18: No discrimination on the basis of sex, religion, political affiliation, sect, colour, caste, creed or ethnic background in enforcing the Act.

Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013). Persons employed in any establishment or industry in Sindh, including fishing and agriculture, with listed exclusions. Official text: https://sindhhighcourt.gov.pk/downloads/source_files/Sindh%20Industrial%20Relation%20Act,%202013.pdf Caveats: Text checked against the High Court of Sindh Judges' Library compilation (September 2014); later amendments and the Sindh Industrial Relations Rules, 2021 have not been reviewed. Trans-provincial establishments may fall under the federal Industrial Relations Act, 2012 (see federal-industrial-relations-2012).

Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.1(3): Applies to persons employed in any establishment or industry in Sindh, including fishing and agriculture; excludes, among others, police and defence services, State administration (other than Railway and Pakistan Post workmen), certain security and fire staff, and non-commercial hospitals/care institutions and non-commercial education or emergency services.

Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.3: Workers may form and join trade unions of their choice without prior authorisation; where women are employed, the union executive must include women in proportion to their employment.

Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.17: Unfair labour practices by employers include refusing to employ, discriminating against, or dismissing, transferring or threatening a worker for being a union member or office-bearer or for union activity.

Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.34(1): A worker can bring a grievance about any right under any law, award or settlement to the employer's notice in writing (personally, or through the shop steward or collective bargaining agent) within 3 months of the day the cause arose.

Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.34(2)-(3): The employer must communicate a written decision within 15 days (within 7 days if the grievance was raised through the shop steward or collective bargaining agent).
Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.34(5): When the matter is taken to the Labour Court, it must decide within 90 days.

Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.34(6): If the employer does not decide in time, or the worker is dissatisfied, the worker may take the matter to the Labour Court within 60 days of the employer's decision or of the end of the reply period.

Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.34(8): Not complying with a Labour Court decision under s.34 within 7 days (or the time set) is punishable with imprisonment up to 3 months, or fine up to Rs 500,000, or both (prosecution on the worker's written complaint).
Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.34(10): Workers with a common grievance arising from a common cause may file a joint application.
Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.45: Labour Courts are presided over by a serving or former District Judge or Additional District Judge.
Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.46(4): No court fee is payable for filing documents in a Labour Court.

Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.47(3): An appeal against a Labour Court's final decision (including under s.34) lies to the Labour Appellate Tribunal within 30 days of communication of the decision.

Sindh Industrial Relations Act, 2013 (Sindh Act No. XXIX of 2013), s.61: A worker may be represented by an office-bearer of the collective bargaining agent; lawyers may appear before the Labour Court or Tribunal with its permission, but not in conciliation proceedings.

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026). Domestic work in or for households across Sindh (child care, elderly care, sick care, natal/post-natal care and ancillary work). Official text: https://pas.gov.pk/uploads/acts/Sindh_Act_No.XVIII_of_2026.pdf Caveats: New law (published June 2026). Dispute Resolution Committees, Inspectors and rules may not be notified yet - confirm the current office with the Sindh Labour Department before naming one.

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.1: Extends to the whole of Sindh and came into force at once. The published s.1(1) calls it the 'Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Bill, 2025' (a drafting slip; the notification publishes it as an Act).

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.3: No child below 16 may work in a household in any capacity; workers under 18 may only do light work that does not harm health or development.

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.4: Harassment complaints by a woman domestic worker against a household or employer (or by female household members against a domestic worker) fall under the Ombudsperson appointed under s.7 of the 2010 workplace harassment law.

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.5: No bonded or forced labour; no discrimination (religion, race, caste, creed, sex, ethnicity, place of birth, domicile, migration, etc.); the worker must be addressed as a 'domestic worker', not a 'servant'; no extra work without free consent and extra pay; dignified working conditions and safety; benefits include social security and old-age benefits.

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.6(1)-(3): Every domestic worker must be given a letter of employment in the prescribed form, with a copy sent to the Inspector (manually or digitally); existing workers were to receive letters within 60 days of the Act's commencement.

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.6(4)-(5): Full-time and live-in workers work only 8 hours a day; no domestic worker may be required to work more than 6 days a week (a 7th day only by mutual agreement, at double wages).

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.7: Festival holidays with full pay according to faith; 6 weeks' paid maternity leave (paid directly by the employer if the worker is not registered with an institution); 10 casual leaves (at most 2 consecutive days) and 8 sick leaves (with a medical certificate) per year on full pay.
Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.9: Wages may not be less than the minimum wage notified under the Sindh Minimum Wages Act, 2015.
Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.10: Live-in workers who choose to live at the workplace must get adequate accommodation and decent living conditions.
Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.11: A yearly medical examination and prescribed vaccinations at the employer's cost.

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.13: Termination requires one month's written notice by either side, or one month's wages (average of the last 3 months) in lieu.

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.14: Wages are due within 5 days after the wage period (which cannot exceed one month); when the employer terminates, earned wages must be paid within 2 working days; payment in coin or currency notes.

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.15: Paying below the minimum wage: fine up to 40% of the unskilled minimum wage plus the shortfall; wage claims are settled as under the Sindh Minimum Wages Act, with appeal to the Labour Court within 30 days.

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.16-20: A Domestic Workers Welfare Fund is created; domestic workers register with the Sindh Employees Social Security Institution and employers register (renewable every 3 years).

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.21-22: Disputes go to a Dispute Resolution Committee notified by the Labour Department and must be presented within 30 days of the dispute arising; appeal to the district Appellate Authority within 30 days of the award. Note: Exact places: s.21(3) proviso - dispute presented within 30 days from the date it arises; s.21(4) - appeal within 30 days of the date the award was made; s.22(1) - the Department appoints an Appellate Authority in each district (re-read 2026-10-17).

Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.25: Employer contraventions are fined up to 25% of the unskilled minimum wage (first offence) or 40% (repeat); knowingly employing a child in breach of s.3 is fined 1 to 2 times the unskilled minimum wage.
Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 (Sindh Act No. XVIII of 2026), s.30: A household may be inspected only after a complaint and on the Dispute Resolution Committee's direction.

Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017). Any industrial, commercial or agricultural establishment, mine, business, trade or workplace where economic activity is carried on, including charitable and welfare organisations. Official text: https://lhr.sindh.gov.pk/storage/rulesRegulations/sQGe6HhiUD1MD0sM2Eh9CkCD28MyOMBc5j6x3Bwf.pdf Caveats: For work inside households, the Sindh Domestic Workers Welfare Act, 2025 sets a higher minimum age of 16 (see sindh-domestic-workers-welfare-2025, s.3).
Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017), s.2: A child is a person under 14; an adolescent is a person aged 14 to under 18.
Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017), s.3(1): No child may be employed or permitted to work in any establishment.

Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017), s.3(2): No adolescent may be employed in hazardous work listed in the Schedule (38 items, including transport, mines and quarries, power-driven cutting machinery, tanning, toxic chemicals, LPG/CNG filling sites, glass furnaces, carpet weaving, stone crushing, lifting 15 kg or more, work at 2 metres height or more, scavenging, building and construction).

Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017), s.7: Adolescents may work at most 3 hours before a 1-hour rest, 7 hours a day including rest, never between 7 pm and 8 am, never overtime, and not in two establishments on the same day.
Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017), s.8: Every adolescent worker gets one whole day off each week.

Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017), s.9(3): The adolescent hours and notice rules (ss.7-9) do not apply where work is done by the occupier with family help, or in Government-recognised skill schools.

Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017), s.14(1): Employing a child: imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs 50,000, or both. In hazardous work: imprisonment up to 3 years and fine of Rs 10,000 to 100,000. In slavery, trafficking, debt bondage, forced labour, sexual exploitation or drug trade: imprisonment of 5 to 10 years and fine of Rs 200,000 to 1,000,000.
Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017), s.14(2): Employing an adolescent in hazardous work: imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to Rs 75,000, or both.
Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017), s.17: Any person, police officer or Labour Inspector may file a complaint; offences are tried by the Labour Court.

Sindh Prohibition of Employment of Children Act, 2017 (Sindh Act No. III of 2017), s.22: The occupier must ensure that working adolescents under 16 (and children acquiring skills) attend compulsory schooling, and keep proof of it.

Sindh Home-Based Workers Act, 2018 (Sindh Act No. XXXVII of 2018). Home-based workers in Sindh. Official text: https://lhr.sindh.gov.pk/storage/rulesRegulations/Wcfe2HxMyMk4Pb2l2R5GmsLQfhrkhkIp3x6HM21B.pdf Caveats: Level B: only the listed points are verified. Read the official text before describing other rights.
Sindh Home-Based Workers Act, 2018 (Sindh Act No. XXXVII of 2018), preamble: Provides for the social protection and rights of home-based workers in Sindh.

Sindh Home-Based Workers Act, 2018 (Sindh Act No. XXXVII of 2018), council-registration: Provides for a Council for Home-Based Workers and for the registration of home-based workers and of employers who engage them.

Sindh Shops and Commercial Establishment Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XII of 2016). Shops and commercial establishments in Sindh. Official text: https://lhr.sindh.gov.pk/storage/rulesRegulations/BGUHOVhjWrpnGye93qff0OTpi7Do5FEtFMk4bSqA.pdf Caveats: Level B: working hours, overtime and leave rules have not been extracted yet - do not quote them.
Sindh Shops and Commercial Establishment Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XII of 2016), s.1(2): Extends to the whole of Sindh.

Sindh Shops and Commercial Establishment Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XII of 2016), preamble: Regulates the hours and other conditions of work and employment of persons employed in shops and commercial establishments in Sindh.

Sindh Factories Act, 2015 (Sindh Act No. XIII of 2016). Factories in Sindh. Official text: https://lhr.sindh.gov.pk/storage/rulesRegulations/vvE55rVbpomC9o6VWibHzoR5ISdxrF8weh1h2oLK.pdf Only the existence and scope of this law are verified; do not describe its sections. Caveats: Level B with no extracted provisions: name the law and link it only. Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.1(2): Extends to the whole of Pakistan.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.2(e): 'Complainant' means any person aggrieved by harassment, including a former employee who was removed, dismissed or resigned, and a parent or guardian where the complainant is a minor.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.2(f): 'Employee' includes regular, contractual, piece-rate, gig, temporary, part-time and freelance workers, and students, performers, artists, sportspersons, interns, trainees, domestic workers, home-based workers and apprentices - paid or unpaid.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.2(h): 'Harassment' means (i) unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favours, stalking or cyber stalking, or other verbal, visual, written or physical conduct of a sexual nature or sexually demeaning attitudes (including gestures) that interfere with work or create an intimidating, hostile or offensive environment, or punishing a refusal or making it a condition of employment; or (ii) discrimination on the basis of gender, whether or not sexual in nature.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.2(n): 'Workplace' covers any place where work or services are performed - including educational institutions, gigs, studios, performance venues, courts, highways and sports facilities - and any situation linked to work outside the office.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.3: Every organisation must constitute a 3-member Inquiry Committee with at least one woman member.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.4(1): Within 3 days of a written complaint, the Inquiry Committee must send the charges to the accused, who has 7 days to submit a written defence (otherwise the inquiry proceeds ex parte).

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.4(3): Inquiry evidence is confidential; both parties may be accompanied by a CBA representative, friend or colleague; no adverse action may be taken against the complainant or witnesses; the employer or accused must not create a hostile environment for the complainant.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.4(4): Findings are due within 30 days. Penalties: minor (censure, withholding promotion or increment, stopping at efficiency bar, recovering compensation from the accused) or major (demotion, compulsory retirement, removal, dismissal, suspension or cancellation of a professional licence, fine - part of which may go to the complainant).

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.6: A party aggrieved by the Competent Authority's decision may appeal to the Ombudsperson within 30 days.
Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.7: Ombudspersons are appointed at both the federal and provincial levels.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.8(1): The complainant may choose to complain either to the Ombudsperson or to the organisation's Inquiry Committee.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.8(2): The Ombudsperson issues a show-cause notice within 3 days of receiving the complaint; the accused must reply within 5 days.
Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.8(6): The Ombudsperson must decide a complaint or appeal within 90 days.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.9: A representation against the Ombudsperson's decision lies to the President (federal) or the Governor (provincial) within 30 days, to be decided within 90 days.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.10: The Ombudsperson has civil-court powers (summons, evidence, inspection of premises, contempt) and can impose the penalties listed in s.4(4).

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), s.11: Employers must adopt the Code of Conduct, form the Inquiry Committee, designate a Competent Authority and display the Code in English and the language of most employees. If they fail, any employee can petition the District Court; the fine is Rs 25,000 to 100,000.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), Schedule (Code): A single incident that makes a person uncomfortable or afraid can be harassment; retaliation (including counter-blast defamation suits) is part of harassment; a delay in reporting does not affect the merits of the case.

Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 (as amended by Act No. V of 2022) (Act No. IV of 2010), forum-choice: FOSPAH's regional offices decide workplace harassment complaints from federal or trans-provincial organisations operating in their region; provincial matters go to the provincial Ombudsperson.

Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 - Section 509 (insulting modesty or causing sexual harassment) (Act XLV of 1860, s.509 as substituted by the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2009), s.509 (punishment): Maximum punishment: imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine up to Rs 500,000, or both.

Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act, 2013 (Sindh) (Sindh Act No. XX of 2013), definitions: The Act's definitions include 'harassment' (by reference to section 509 of the Pakistan Penal Code) among the abuse it covers.

Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act, 2013 (Sindh) (Sindh Act No. XX of 2013), protection-committees: Government constitutes Protection Committees (including a Social Welfare Officer) for the purposes of the Act.

Establishment of the Office of Ombudsman for the Province of Sindh Act, 1991, jurisdiction: The Provincial Ombudsman (Mohtasib) Sindh investigates complaints of maladministration - decisions contrary to law, arbitrary, biased or discriminatory acts, corruption or favouritism, neglect, delay or inefficiency - by Sindh Government departments and institutions.

Establishment of the Office of Ombudsman for the Province of Sindh Act, 1991, procedure: Complaints may be made in English, Urdu or Sindhi - online, by email, by post or in person. First approach the agency's higher authorities, and attach that correspondence and a copy of the CNIC.
Establishment of the Office of Ombudsman for the Province of Sindh Act, 1991, cost: The Ombudsman's services are free; anonymous complaints are not investigated.

Establishment of the Office of Ombudsman for the Province of Sindh Act, 1991, s.10(3): A complaint must be made within 3 months from the day the aggrieved person first had notice of the matter complained of. The Ombudsman may still take up a late complaint if there are special circumstances. Note: Section number and wording from the 1991 Ordinance that preceded the Act; the Ombudsman's official flyer states the same 3-month limit.

Establishment of the Office of Ombudsman for the Province of Sindh Act, 1991, s.32: A person aggrieved by a decision or order of the Ombudsman may make a representation to the Governor of Sindh within 30 days of the decision or order. Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979). Rented premises (buildings or land, not hotels) in urban areas of Sindh, except premises owned or requisitioned by the Federal or Provincial Government. Official text: https://sja.gos.pk/assets/Updated_Laws/Sindh%20Rented%20Premises%20Ordinance,1979.pdf Caveats: First check the location: cantonment areas are governed by the Cantonments Rent Restriction Act, 1963 (see cantonments-rent-restriction-1963); Islamabad by the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance, 2001. Workers living in employer-provided housing: see Standing Order 22 (sindh-standing-orders-2015). Security deposit refunds are not dealt with in this compiled text (s.6 was omitted in 1984) - refer the user to SLACC rather than inventing a rule.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.2: 'Landlord' includes anyone entitled to receive the rent; 'tenant' includes a person still in possession after the tenancy ends and heirs in possession; 'premises' means a building or land let on rent, excluding hotels; 'personal use' means use by the owner or the owner's spouse, son or daughter.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.3: Applies to all premises in urban areas (within a Town Committee, Municipal Committee, Municipal Corporation or Metropolitan Corporation) except premises owned or requisitioned by the Federal or Provincial Government; Government may exclude premises or areas by notification.
Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.4: Rent Controllers - judicial officers with at least 3 years as Civil Judge - are appointed for each district.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.5: Every tenancy agreement must be in writing; if it is not compulsorily registrable, it must be attested by the Rent Controller, a Civil Judge or a First Class Magistrate. The registered or attested deed is the accepted proof of the landlord-tenant relationship.
Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.7: A landlord cannot charge more than the agreed rent, or more than the fair rent once the Controller has fixed it.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.8: On application by the tenant or the landlord, the Controller fixes the fair rent, considering rents of similar nearby premises, rising construction and repair costs, new taxes, and the annual value used for property tax.
Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.9: Once fair rent is fixed, it cannot be increased for 3 years; an increase may not exceed 10% per year of the existing rent.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.10: Unless agreed otherwise, rent is due by the 10th of the following month; the landlord must give a written receipt. If the landlord refuses or avoids taking rent, the tenant may send it by postal money order or deposit it with the Rent Controller - these receipts are proof of payment.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.11: A landlord may not cut off electricity, gas, water or similar services without the tenant's consent, an authority's requisition or the Controller's direction. The tenant can apply to the Controller for restoration, and the landlord is punishable with simple imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine, or both.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.12: If the landlord fails to carry out necessary repairs or whitewashing, the Controller may allow the tenant to do it and deduct the cost from the rent.
Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.13: No tenant can be evicted except in accordance with this Ordinance.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.14: A landlord who is a widow, a minor whose parents are both dead, a salaried employee retiring within 6 months or already retired, or a person who is (or within 6 months will be) 60, may demand vacant possession for personal use by written notice of at least 2 months. This is not available if the building was let after retirement, turning 60 or being widowed or orphaned, or if the landlord already occupies a building they own. The Controller then orders eviction summarily.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.15(2): The Controller orders eviction only if satisfied that: the tenant did not pay rent within 15 days after the agreed due date, or within 60 days of it falling due if there is no agreement (a first default of up to 6 months, admitted at the first hearing, can be cured by paying); without written consent the tenant sublet or handed over possession, changed the use, or breached the tenancy conditions; the tenant impaired the value or utility of the premises; the tenant caused nuisance to neighbours; the landlord has sanction to reconstruct; or the landlord genuinely needs it for own use or the use of spouse or children.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.15(3)-(4), s.15-A: If a landlord who obtained possession for reconstruction does not demolish within 6 months or start building within 2 years, or re-lets or does not personally use premises taken for personal use within a year, the evicted tenant can apply to be restored; misuse of a personal-use eviction is fined up to one year's rent.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.16: Once an eviction case is filed, the Controller may order the tenant to deposit arrears and then monthly rent by the 10th of each month; if the tenant fails, the defence is struck off and possession is ordered.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.17: If an eviction application is frivolous or vexatious, the Controller may order the landlord to pay the tenant compensation of up to 10 times the monthly rent.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.18: When ownership changes, the new owner must inform the tenant in writing by registered post; the tenant is not in default if the rent is paid within 30 days of when that notice would normally have arrived.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.19: A respondent gets up to 15 days from the notice to file a written reply; evidence is given by affidavit with cross-examination.

Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.21: An appeal against a final (not interim) order of the Controller lies to the District Judge within 30 days; the appellate order is final.
Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.22: Final orders are executed by the Controller, not through a separate suit.
Sind Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (Sind Ordinance No. XVII of 1979), s.24: Courts take cognizance of offences under the Ordinance only on the Controller's written complaint.

Cantonments Rent Restriction Act, 1963, s.24: Appeals (First Rent Appeals) against the Controller's orders are heard by the High Court of Sindh.

[Legal basis: Payment of Wages Act s.15(1); Payment of Wages Act s.15(2)] [Contact: Labour & Human Resources Department, Government of Sindh 021-99211551]

Fired, terminated or forced out of a job. Applies when: Worker in an industrial or commercial establishment in Sindh with 10 or more workers.
Step 1 (legal): Check the worker's class: permanent (long-term work, after completing 3 months' probation) or probationer, temporary, badli or contract. [Legal basis: Standing Orders Act s.1(4); Standing Orders Act SO 1]
Step 2 (legal): A permanent worker terminated for a reason other than misconduct must get one month's notice or one month's wages in lieu. Temporary, probationer, badli and contract workers are not entitled to notice. [Legal basis: Standing Orders Act SO 16(1); Standing Orders Act SO 16(2)]
Step 3 (legal): Termination must be by a written order that states the reason - ask for it in writing. [Legal basis: Standing Orders Act SO 16(3)]
Step 4 (legal): Dismissal for misconduct requires a written charge within one month, a chance to explain and an independent inquiry; suspension cannot exceed 4 weeks in total and is on full pay. [Legal basis: Standing Orders Act SO 21(3); Standing Orders Act SO 21(4); Standing Orders Act SO 21(5)]
Step 5 (legal): Final wages and dues are due within 2 working days; gratuity of one month's wages per completed year (unless dismissed for misconduct or covered by a matching provident fund); the full provident fund balance; and a service certificate for permanent workers. [Legal basis: Standing Orders Act SO 16(4); Standing Orders Act SO 16(6); Standing Orders Act SO 16(7); Standing Orders Act SO 17]
Step 6 (legal): If the worker is stopped from entering or marking attendance, report it in writing to the area Inspector within 10 days. [Legal basis: Standing Orders Act SO 16(10)] [Contact: Labour & Human Resources Department, Government of Sindh 021-99211551]
Step 7 (legal): Send a written grievance notice to the employer within 3 months; the employer must reply in writing within 15 days. [Legal basis: SIRA 2013 s.34(1); SIRA 2013 s.34(2)-(3)]
Step 8 (legal): If there is no reply or it is unsatisfactory, file in the Labour Court within 60 days. No court fee; the Labour Court should decide within 90 days. [Legal basis: SIRA 2013 s.34(6); SIRA 2013 s.46(4); SIRA 2013 s.34(5)]
Step 9 (legal): Appeal against the Labour Court's decision to the Labour Appellate Tribunal within 30 days. [Legal basis: SIRA 2013 s.47(3)]
Step 10 (contact): Get free legal advice before sending the grievance notice. [Contact: Sindh Legal Advisory Call Center (SLACC) - Legal Aid Society 0800-70806]
Deadline - Report to the Inspector if not allowed to work: 10 days [Standing Orders Act SO 16(10)]
Deadline - Grievance notice to the employer: 3 months from the cause [SIRA 2013 s.34(1)]
Deadline - Employer's written reply: 15 days (7 days if via shop steward/CBA) [SIRA 2013 s.34(2)-(3)]
Deadline - Filing in the Labour Court: 60 days after the reply or the end of the reply period [SIRA 2013 s.34(6)]
Deadline - Appeal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal: 30 days [SIRA 2013 s.47(3)]
Caveats: Standing Orders apply only where 10 or more workers are employed. Dismissal because of union membership or activity is an unfair labour practice (SIRA s.17). Trans-provincial employers: federal IRA 2012 and the NIRC may apply (federal-industrial-relations-2012).

Step 1 (legal): What counts: unwelcome sexual advances or requests, stalking or cyber stalking, sexual conduct or demeaning attitudes, and discrimination because of gender. A single incident can count, and retaliation is also harassment. [Legal basis: Workplace Harassment Act s.2(h); Workplace Harassment Act Schedule (Code)]
Step 2 (legal): Who is protected: any person - including contract, part-time, gig and freelance workers, interns, students, domestic and home-based workers, and former employees. [Legal basis: Workplace Harassment Act s.2(e); Workplace Harassment Act s.2(f); Workplace Harassment Act s.2(n)]
Step 3 (legal): Choose the forum: the organisation's Inquiry Committee, or directly the Ombudsperson. [Legal basis: Workplace Harassment Act s.8(1); Workplace Harassment Act s.3]
Step 4 (legal): Which Ombudsperson: provincial and private organisations in Sindh go to the Provincial Ombudsman Sindh; federal or trans-provincial organisations go to FOSPAH (Karachi regional office). [Legal basis: Workplace Harassment Act s.7; Workplace Harassment Act forum-choice] [Contact: Provincial Ombudsman Sindh (Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace); Federal Ombudsperson Secretariat for Protection Against Harassment (FOSPAH) 0344-4367367]
Step 5 (legal): Timelines: the Inquiry Committee sends charges within 3 days, the accused replies within 7 days, findings within 30 days. The Ombudsperson issues notice within 3 days, the accused replies within 5 days, and the decision is due within 90 days. [Legal basis: Workplace Harassment Act s.4(1); Workplace Harassment Act s.4(4); Workplace Harassment Act s.8(2); Workplace Harassment Act s.8(6)]
Step 6 (legal): Protection: no adverse action may be taken against the complainant or witnesses, and inquiry evidence is confidential. [Legal basis: Workplace Harassment Act s.4(3)]
Step 7 (legal): Appeals: the Competent Authority's decision can be appealed to the Ombudsperson within 30 days; the Ombudsperson's decision can be challenged before the Governor (provincial) or President (federal) within 30 days. [Legal basis: Workplace Harassment Act s.6; Workplace Harassment Act s.9]
Step 8 (legal): A criminal complaint is possible at the same time: sexual harassment is an offence under s.509 PPC (up to 3 years' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to Rs 500,000). [Legal basis: PPC 509 s.509; PPC 509 s.509 (punishment)] [Contact: Sindh Police Emergency Helpline (Madadgar 15) 15]
Step 9 (practical tip): Write down dates, what happened and witnesses; keep screenshots and messages.
Deadline - Appeal against the Competent Authority's decision: 30 days [Workplace Harassment Act s.6]
Deadline - Representation against the Ombudsperson's decision: 30 days [Workplace Harassment Act s.9]

Landlord wants to evict the tenant. Applies when: Rented premises in an urban area of Sindh (not a cantonment, not Government-owned).
Step 1 (legal): Check the location first: urban areas of Sindh fall under the SRPO 1979; cantonment areas fall under the Cantonments Rent Restriction Act, 1963. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.3; Cantonment Rent Act scope]
Step 2 (legal): No tenant can be evicted except under the Ordinance - that is, through an order of the Rent Controller. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.13]
Step 3 (legal): The landlord must prove a ground before the Controller: rent default (15 days after the agreed date, or 60 days if no agreed date), subletting or change of use or breach without written consent, damage, nuisance, sanctioned reconstruction, or genuine personal need. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.15(2)]
Step 4 (legal): Exception: a widow, an orphaned minor, a retiring or retired salaried person, or a landlord aged 60+ can demand vacant possession for personal use with at least 2 months' written notice. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.14]
Step 5 (legal): If a case is filed: reply within the time in the notice (at most 15 days), and obey any order to deposit arrears and monthly rent by the 10th - otherwise the defence is struck off. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.19; SRPO 1979 s.16]
Step 6 (legal): If the landlord's application is frivolous or vexatious, the Controller may award the tenant up to 10 months' rent as compensation. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.17]
Step 7 (legal): Appeal against the Controller's final order to the District Judge within 30 days. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.21]
Step 8 (legal): If the landlord took possession for personal use or reconstruction and then misuses it, the tenant can apply to be restored. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.15(3)-(4), s.15-A]
Step 9 (practical tip): If the landlord uses force, threats or a lock-out, call police 15 and get legal advice; keep the rent agreement and all rent receipts. [Contact: Sindh Police Emergency Helpline (Madadgar 15) 15; Sindh Legal Advisory Call Center (SLACC) - Legal Aid Society 0800-70806]
Deadline - Written reply to the Controller's notice: Within the period in the notice (not more than 15 days) [SRPO 1979 s.19]
Deadline - Appeal to the District Judge: 30 days from the Controller's final order [SRPO 1979 s.21]
Caveats: A worker living in employer-provided housing must vacate within 2 months after the job ends (Standing Order 22) - different rules. Cantonment areas: see cantonments-rent-restriction-1963.

Landlord refuses to take rent or give a receipt. Applies when: Rented premises governed by the SRPO 1979.
Step 1 (legal): Unless agreed otherwise, rent is due by the 10th of the following month and the landlord must give a written receipt. If the landlord refuses or avoids taking rent, send it by postal money order or deposit it with the Rent Controller - those receipts prove payment. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.10]
Step 2 (legal): This matters because non-payment within 15 days of the agreed date (or 60 days if none) is a ground for eviction. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.15(2)]
Step 3 (legal): If the property was sold or inherited, the new owner must notify the tenant by registered post; rent paid within 30 days of that notice is not a default. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.18]

Rent increase and fair rent. Applies when: Rented premises governed by the SRPO 1979.
Step 1 (legal): A landlord cannot charge more than the agreed rent, or more than the fair rent once fixed by the Controller. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.7]
Step 2 (legal): Either the tenant or the landlord can apply to the Rent Controller to fix the fair rent (based on similar nearby rents, costs, taxes and the property's annual value). [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.8]
Step 3 (legal): Once fair rent is fixed it cannot be raised for 3 years, and an increase may not exceed 10% a year of the existing rent. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.9] [Contact: Sindh Legal Advisory Call Center (SLACC) - Legal Aid Society 0800-70806]
Caveats: How the 10% cap applies to increases written into a private rent agreement (where no fair rent was fixed) should be confirmed by a lawyer - do not state it as settled.

Rent agreement and police tenant registration. Applies when: Renting premises in Sindh.
Step 1 (legal): The tenancy agreement must be in writing; if it is not compulsorily registrable, it must be attested by the Rent Controller, a Civil Judge or a First Class Magistrate. This deed is the proof of tenancy. [Legal basis: SRPO 1979 s.5]
Step 2 (legal): The landlord, tenant and property dealer must give the tenant's information to the police. [Legal basis: Tenant Registration Act information-to-police]
Step 3 (legal): Registration is free at the police station or facilitation centre (owner's and tenant's CNICs, rent agreement, affidavit, tenant's photo), or online on TRUST. [Legal basis: Tenant Registration Act procedure (Karachi Police)] [Contact: Tenant Registration - Karachi / Sindh Police (TRUST portal)]
Caveats: Deadlines and penalties under the tenant registration law have not been extracted - do not state them.

Need free legal advice or a free lawyer. Applies when: Anyone who cannot afford a lawyer.
Step 1 (contact): Call the Sindh Legal Advisory Call Center for free legal advice (24/7). The Legal Aid Society also takes up some cases for free representation. [Contact: Sindh Legal Advisory Call Center (SLACC) - Legal Aid Society 0800-70806]
Step 2 (contact): For human rights violations, the Ministry of Human Rights helpline 1099 gives free legal advice and referrals. [Contact: Ministry of Human Rights - Helpline 1099 (legal advice on human rights violations) 1099]
Step 3 (legal): If a case is in court: ask the District Legal Empowerment Committee at the District & Sessions Court for free legal representation. [Legal basis: DLEC Rules purpose] [Contact: District Legal Empowerment Committee (DLEC) - free legal representation through the district court]
Step 4 (legal): The Pakistan Bar Council accepts free legal aid applications online. [Legal basis: PBC Free Legal Aid Rules application] [Contact: Pakistan Bar Council - Free Legal Aid (Central Free Legal Aid Committee)]
Caveats: LAJA (federal Legal Aid and Justice Authority) exists, but no official contact was verified - do not give a LAJA phone number.

Complaint against a Sindh Government department. Applies when: Maladministration by a Sindh Government department or institution.
Step 1 (legal): First approach the department's higher authority in writing. [Legal basis: Sindh Ombudsman Act procedure]
Step 2 (legal): Then complain to the Provincial Ombudsman (Mohtasib) Sindh within 3 months of first learning of the problem (a late complaint is taken up only in special circumstances) - free; in English, Urdu or Sindhi; online, email, post or in person; attach the correspondence and a CNIC copy. Anonymous complaints are not investigated. [Legal basis: Sindh Ombudsman Act jurisdiction; Sindh Ombudsman Act procedure; Sindh Ombudsman Act cost; Sindh Ombudsman Act s.10(3)] [Contact: Provincial Ombudsman (Mohtasib) Sindh 021-99211026]
Step 3 (legal): If you disagree with the Ombudsman's decision, a representation can be made to the Governor of Sindh within 30 days of the decision - count from the date of the decision, not from when you received it. [Legal basis: Sindh Ombudsman Act s.32]
Step 4 (contact): Other channels: the Chief Minister's public complaint cell; for human rights violations, the Human Rights Department complaint cell. [Contact: Sindh Chief Minister's Public Complaint Cell 0800-91915; Human Rights Complaint Cell - Human Rights Department, Government of Sindh 0800-00011]
Deadline - Complaint to the Provincial Ombudsman (Mohtasib) Sindh: 3 months from the day you first learned of the matter (late complaints only in special circumstances) [Sindh Ombudsman Act s.10(3)]
Deadline - Representation to the Governor against the Ombudsman's decision: 30 days from the date of the decision or order [Sindh Ombudsman Act s.32]

Complaint about police conduct. Applies when: Police in Sindh.
Step 1 (contact): Complain to the IGP Complaint Cell (1715) or to CPLC (24/7 helpline 1102, or its online report form). [Contact: Inspector General of Police Complaint Cell, Sindh Police 1715; Citizens-Police Liaison Committee (CPLC) 1102]
Step 2 (contact): For human rights violations, also complain to the Human Rights Department complaint cell or the Sindh Human Rights Commission. [Contact: Human Rights Complaint Cell - Human Rights Department, Government of Sindh 0800-00011; Sindh Human Rights Commission (SHRC) 021-99217318]
Step 3 (contact): Get free legal advice on next steps. [Contact: Sindh Legal Advisory Call Center (SLACC) - Legal Aid Society 0800-70806]

Domestic violence or a woman in danger. Applies when: Sindh.
Step 1 (contact): In immediate danger, call police emergency 15. [Contact: Sindh Police Emergency Helpline (Madadgar 15) 15]
Step 2 (contact): Women Development Department helpline 1094 takes complaints of women facing violence; it also runs district women complaint cells and shelters (Darul Aman, safe houses). [Contact: Women Development Department Sindh - Women Helpline 1094 1094]
Step 3 (contact): Madadgar helpline 1098 for women protection. [Contact: Women Protection Unit - Madadgar (LHRLA), Helpline 1098 1098]
Step 4 (legal): Sindh has a Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act, 2013 whose definitions cover harassment among other abuse; for remedies under it, get legal advice. [Legal basis: Sindh Domestic Violence Act s.1(2); Sindh Domestic Violence Act definitions] [Contact: Sindh Legal Advisory Call Center (SLACC) - Legal Aid Society 0800-70806]
